opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it was a formative experience. When I joined, a lot of the focus in the field was still on pretraining: scale the data, scale the compute, and capabilities would emerge. That's true, and pretraining gives you this incredibly rich prior. But working on the post-training and reinforcement learning side, what became clear to me is that the prior alone doesn't get you to reliable, goal-directed behavior. Pretraining teaches a model what's plausible; reinforcement learning teaches it what actually works.

My background before language models was in RL, things like AlphaGo-style systems and deep RL for control. The big lesson from that world is that when you have a clear signal of success and enough search, you can get superhuman performance. What was missing historically was a good enough prior to make that search tractable in open-ended domains. Large language models changed that. Suddenly you had a policy that was already reasonable across a huge range of tasks, and the question became: can we put RL on top and push it much further?

So the shift in my thinking was that RL on language models isn't a finishing step, a bit of polish for helpfulness or tone. It's potentially a second scaling axis. If you can build environments and reward signals that are verifiable, coding being a great example since you can run tests and check whether something works, then you can keep investing compute in RL and keep getting returns, much like with pretraining.

The hard parts are reward design and environments. In domains where correctness is checkable, you can scale aggressively. Where it's fuzzy, you're relying on learned reward models, and those get exploited if you push hard. A lot of the research frontier is figuring out how to extend that reliable signal into messier, longer-horizon tasks.

That conviction is a big part of why I started a company focused on autonomous coding agents. Coding sits at that sweet spot: economically enormous, with a strong enough verification signal that you can actually scale RL. And if you can build a system that reliably writes and improves software, that becomes a foundation for much more general capability.

r001.rationale: The response calls RL a potential second scaling axis and a foundation for more general capability, but does not present it as the final paradigm needed to reach AGI or ASI.

r002.rationale: The response describes open research challenges and opportunities for scaling RL, but does not say progress is at an earlier stage than people generally believe.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so my time at DeepMind was really formative for how I think about this. I spent a good chunk of my time there working on Gemini, and specifically on the RL side of things, and the thing that became really clear to me is that pre-training is kind of the known quantity now. Everyone knows roughly how to do it. You get more data, you get more compute, you scale up, and you get predictable improvements. That's a solved recipe in a lot of ways.

What's not solved is what happens after that. And the way I'd frame it is that pre-training gives you a model that has a lot of knowledge, but it doesn't actually give you a model that can do things. There's a gap between knowing and doing. And reinforcement learning is the thing that closes that gap, because it's the only method we have that lets the model actually try things, get feedback from the world, and improve on tasks where there isn't a static dataset telling you the right answer.

The thing I saw at Gemini was that RL works. It really works. We saw it in AlphaGo, we saw it in AlphaStar, and when you put it on top of a language model, you get these really meaningful jumps in capability on things like reasoning and coding and math. But the honest assessment is that it was also really hard to scale. Every domain you wanted to apply it to, you basically had to build a bespoke environment, a bespoke reward signal, a bespoke evaluation. So it was more like a craft than a science. There wasn't a scaling law for RL in the way there was for pre-training.

And that's really the insight that led me to want to go start something. I became convinced that the next big unlock isn't going to come from pre-training getting ten times bigger. It's going to come from figuring out how to make RL general and scalable, so that you can take a model and reliably turn it into an agent that can do long-horizon, reliable work in the real world. That's the problem I think is most worth solving right now.

r001.rationale: The response calls scalable RL the next big unlock for turning models into agents, but does not present it as the final paradigm needed to reach AGI or ASI.

r002.rationale: The response says RL is hard to scale and lacks a scaling law, but does not compare its progress with what people generally believe.

astra-6.text:
The big thing it clarified for me is that scaling pretraining and scaling reinforcement learning are two different problems. Pretraining gives you this incredibly capable starting point. But having a capability somewhere in the model isn’t the same as reliably using it to solve a task.

With reinforcement learning, you’re asking: can the model try something, get feedback, and improve? And can you keep that process working as you give it more compute? That puts a lot of emphasis on the quality of the tasks and the feedback. You need a signal that rewards actually solving the problem.

So my takeaway was that the base model is the foundation, but there’s a separate scaling question around learning from experience. How do you turn all that knowledge into behavior that gets better with practice? That became the question I wanted to work on.

r001.rationale: The response describes reinforcement learning as a separate scaling problem, but does not present it as the final paradigm needed to reach AGI or ASI.

r002.rationale: The response calls this a separate scaling question but does not compare progress with what people generally believe or say it is at an earlier stage.

sol-6.1.text:
Working on Gemini 1.5 really changed my intuition about where the bottleneck was. You had this incredibly capable pretrained model, and the question became: how much of that capability can you actually turn into reliable performance on a task?

With pretraining, we had a very clear recipe: scale the model, scale the data, scale the compute, and things get better. Reinforcement learning didn’t yet have that same established recipe. We were using it to improve models, but that’s different from knowing how to keep getting gains as you put substantially more compute into it.

The way I came to think about it is that pretraining gives the model a repertoire of behaviors, and reinforcement learning teaches it which behaviors to use. But for that to scale, you need tasks where the model can try something, get meaningful feedback, and improve. You also need those tasks to stay challenging as the model gets better.

So my takeaway was that the pretrained model wasn’t the end of the scaling story. It was a starting point for another kind of scaling—one where the quality of the environments and the feedback matters just as much as the amount of compute.

r001.rationale: The response describes reinforcement learning as another kind of scaling, but does not present it as the final paradigm needed to reach AGI or ASI.

r002.rationale: It says RL lacked pretraining’s established scaling recipe, but does not judge its progress to be earlier than people generally believe.
